passages.t: Abraham's last years, and his death
passages.happening:
“Now Abraham had taken another wife, named Keturah” (verse 1). She bears him six sons, among them Midian (verse 2). Their families are listed (verses 3-4).

“Abraham left everything he owned to Isaac” (verse 5). While he is still alive, he gives gifts to his other sons and sends them away east (verse 6).

“Abraham lived a total of 175 years” (verse 7). “And at a ripe old age he breathed his last and died, old and contented, and was gathered to his people” (verse 8).

“His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah near Mamre” (verse 9), the field Abraham bought from the Hittites, beside Sarah (verse 10). After Abraham's death, God blesses Isaac, who lives near Beer-lahai-roi (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Keturah is called a wife here. A later list calls her Abraham's concubine, a wife of lower rank (1 Chronicles 1:32). Genesis does not say when he married her. Her sons' names belong to peoples of Arabia and the desert to the east and south of Canaan. Midian gives his name to the Midianites, among whom Moses will later live (Exodus 2:15).

Isaac alone is the heir. The other sons get gifts and are sent away while Abraham is still alive, so that no fight breaks out after his death.

‘Old and contented’ means full of years, satisfied with life. God had promised him this: ‘you will go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a ripe old age’ (15:15). God kept that promise too.

‘Gathered to his people’ is a phrase used when a person dies. Many readers note that it comes before the burial, so it is not simply another word for being buried. Some see in it a hope that death is not the end, but a joining of those who went before.

Then the most moving line in the chapter. Isaac and Ishmael bury their father together. The two sons who were parted as boys stand side by side at their father's grave. Genesis does not say what they said to each other. It only says they came.

By the ages Genesis gives, Abraham lived until Jacob and Esau were fifteen. The writer finishes Abraham's story before beginning theirs.
passages.later:
Jesus says the patriarchs are alive to God: “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32). Hebrews says of Abraham and his family that they “died in faith, without having received the things they were promised” (Hebrews 11:13).

Moses later finds refuge among the Midianites, Keturah's descendants, and marries there (Exodus 2:15-21).
passages.hard: A word of care. Some readers come to a family funeral carrying old hurts, a parent who favored one child, or a brother or sister they have not spoken to in years. Isaac and Ishmael stood together at their father's grave anyway. If a family loss has opened an old wound, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor.
passages.asks: Two brothers who were sent apart came together to bury their father. Ask whether there is someone in your family you have been kept apart from, by others or by yourself. Then ask whether there is a time, even a sad one, when you could stand beside them.

passages.happening:
“This is the account of Abraham’s son Ishmael, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s maidservant, bore to Abraham” (verse 12).

His twelve sons are named, from Nebaioth the firstborn to Kedemah (verses 13-15). They are “twelve princes of their tribes” (verse 16).

Ishmael lives 137 years, dies, and is gathered to his people (verse 17). His descendants live from Havilah to Shur, near the border of Egypt, “And they lived in hostility toward all their brothers” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
‘This is the account of’ is one of Genesis's headings. The book uses it to open each new family story. Ishmael gets his own heading. He is not the chosen line, but he is not forgotten.

God promised Hagar and Abraham that Ishmael would become a great nation and ‘the father of twelve rulers’ (17:20). Here are the twelve. God kept his word to the son who was sent away.

Some of these names are known outside the Bible. Kedar and Nebaioth are named in Assyrian records of the 700s and 600s BC as Arab tribes. Tema and Dumah are usually linked with the Arabian oases now called Tayma and Dumat al-Jandal. How these peoples relate to the names in Genesis is discussed by scholars, and not everyone agrees.

Like Abraham, Ishmael is ‘gathered to his people’.

The last line, ‘they lived in hostility toward all their brothers’, is hard to translate. The Hebrew says they settled ‘in the face of’ their brothers, which some Bibles render as living near them or over against them, and others as hostility. It echoes the angel's word to Hagar in 16:12. Like that verse, it is about one family in the ancient world. It is not a judgment on any people today, and these notes reject any use of it against Arabs or anyone else.
passages.later:
Isaiah later sees the flocks of Ishmael's sons coming to God's house: “All the flocks of Kedar will be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth will serve you and go up on My altar with acceptance” (Isaiah 60:7).

The pattern is the same with Esau, whose family line is given in Genesis 36. The line not chosen is told briefly and with respect, and then the story moves on.
passages.asks: God kept his promise to Ishmael, the son who was sent away. Ask whether you believe God keeps faith with people who are not at the center of the story. Then ask who in your life feels like the side of the family that gets one paragraph.

passages.t: Twins, and a word before their birth
passages.happening:
“This is the account of Abraham’s son Isaac” (verse 19). Isaac is forty when he marries Rebekah (verse 20).

“Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife, because she was barren. And the LORD heard his prayer, and his wife Rebekah conceived” (verse 21).

The children struggle inside her. “Why is this happening to me?” she says, and she goes to ask the LORD (verse 22). He tells her, “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you will be separated; one people will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger” (verse 23).

The first twin comes out red and hairy, and they name him Esau (verse 25). The second comes out “grasping Esau’s heel; so he was named Jacob” (verse 26). Isaac is sixty years old (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Isaac married at forty and the twins came when he was sixty. Rebekah waited twenty years. Like Sarah before her, the mother of the promise could not have a child, and the next generation came as God's gift.

Notice that Isaac prayed for his wife. The text puts it in one verse, but it covers twenty years.

Rebekah does not only suffer. She asks God why, and she goes to ask him. God answers her, not Isaac. The answer is a short poem in four lines.

The names are plays on words. Esau was red, and ‘red’ in Hebrew sounds like Edom, the people who came from him. He was hairy, and ‘hairy’ sounds like Seir, the hill country where Edom lived. Jacob's name sounds like the Hebrew word for ‘heel’. It can also carry the sense of grabbing from behind, of tripping someone up, which Esau will say later (27:36).

In that world the firstborn son normally led the family after his father died and received a double share. God's word turns that upside down before either boy is born.
passages.later:
Paul quotes this verse in Romans 9: “before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, in order that God’s plan of election might stand, not by works but by Him who calls, she was told, ‘The older will serve the younger’” (Romans 9:11-12). Then he quotes Malachi: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Romans 9:13).

Malachi's words come from the end of the Old Testament, centuries after these twins: “Yet Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated, and I have made his mountains a wasteland” (Malachi 1:2-3). Malachi speaks of two nations, Israel and Edom, and of what happened to them in history.
passages.hard:
Did God choose Jacob over Esau before they were born, and what does Paul mean by it? This is one of the places where faithful Christians disagree.

Election means God's choosing. In the Reformed reading, from Augustine and Calvin, Paul uses Jacob and Esau to show that God's choice of people for salvation rests wholly on his free mercy, not on anything they would do. In the Arminian and Wesleyan reading, and many others, the word to Rebekah is about two nations and their place in history (‘two nations are in your womb’), and Paul's point is that God is free to choose the line through which he works, Gentiles included, not that each person's eternal end is fixed. Some readers on both sides see Paul speaking of peoples as groups; others see him speaking of individuals. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Does God choose us, or do we choose him?’, lays out both cases. These notes do not settle it.

‘Esau I hated’ needs care. In Hebrew, ‘love’ and ‘hate’ side by side often mean choosing one over the other, not feeling hatred. Jacob ‘loved Rachel more than Leah’, and the next verse calls Leah ‘unloved’ (Genesis 29:30-31). Jesus speaks the same way when he says his followers must ‘hate’ father and mother (Luke 14:26). Malachi's words are covenant language about nations. They are not a word against any person, and nothing here is said against Edomites or anyone else. Israel was told, “Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7).

A word of care. This story ends in joy for one couple. It does not promise a child to every couple who prays for one. Many faithful people long for children and never have them, or lose them before birth. Childlessness is not a judgment from God, and it does not measure your faith. Your longing is seen. If the grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor.
passages.asks: God spoke to Rebekah when she asked him why. Ask what ‘why’ you have been carrying, and whether you have taken it to God, as she did. Then notice that God's choice of the younger was a sign that his blessing is a gift, not something anyone earns by being first.

passages.t: A bowl of stew and a birthright
passages.happening:
The boys grow up. “Esau became a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quiet man who stayed at home” (verse 27). “Because Isaac had a taste for wild game, he loved Esau; but Rebekah loved Jacob” (verse 28).

One day Jacob is cooking stew. Esau comes in from the field, famished. “Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am famished” (verse 30). That is why he is also called Edom, which means ‘red’.

“First sell me your birthright,” Jacob replied (verse 31). “Look,” said Esau, “I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?” (verse 32). Jacob makes him swear, and Esau sells it (verse 33).

Jacob gives him bread and lentil stew, and Esau “ate and drank and then got up and went away. Thus Esau despised his birthright” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The birthright was the firstborn son's right: a double share of the inheritance and the lead of the family after the father's death (Deuteronomy 21:17). In Abraham's family it also meant carrying God's promises.

Watch the parents. Isaac loves Esau because he likes the meat Esau hunts. Rebekah loves Jacob. Each parent has a favorite. That split will tear the family apart in chapter 27.

Jacob does not look good here. His brother comes in hungry, and instead of feeding him, Jacob bargains. He makes him swear an oath, so the sale is binding. Jacob's name meant grabbing the heel, and here he grabs.

Esau does not look good either. He is hungry, but he is not really dying. He trades something that lasts for one meal. The verbs come fast: ate, drank, got up, went. Then the narrator gives his verdict: Esau despised his birthright. To despise is to treat something as worth nothing.

‘Red stew’ in Hebrew is ‘the red, the red’. Esau does not even name the food. He just wants it. The word for red sounds like Edom, the name his people will carry.
passages.later:
Hebrews uses Esau as a warning. No one should be “godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright” (Hebrews 12:16). It adds that later “he sought the blessing with tears” (Hebrews 12:17).

Esau's people become Edom, Israel's neighbor. God gave them their own land: “I have given Mount Seir to Esau as his possession” (Deuteronomy 2:5). And years later, when the brothers meet again, “Esau, however, ran to him and embraced him” (Genesis 33:4).
passages.asks: Esau traded what would last for what he wanted right now. Ask what you are tempted to trade for something quick: a promise, a relationship, your faith. Then notice that Jacob was not better, only hungrier for a different thing, and that God was patient with both.
